one_liner: A command-line self-test that sends known-destructive tool calls through your own Claude Code guard hooks, without running them, and prints which ones your hooks blocked and which got through.
who: A developer who has layered guard hooks into Claude Code from two plugins and is about to let the agent run unattended.
moment: Before letting the agent run unattended, they want to know whether force-pushes and secret writes are actually blocked, and they do not want to find out on a real repo.
why_now: Guard-hook plugins like skillkeel-starter are shipping now (v0.1.12 on 2026-10-11). A benchmark of harness security mechanisms, HarnessSecurity-Bench, appeared on 2026-10-06 and names the attack surfaces. A developer asked how to verify stacked hooks on 2026-10-12.

existing.name: skillkeel-starter
existing.does: MIT Claude Code plugin with three guard hooks blocking destructive commands, force-pushes and secret writes; its skills have fixture-repo evals
existing.lacks: A test of the user's whole installed hook stack across plugins, and a pass/fail report on what a given config lets through

existing.name: HarnessSecurity-Bench
existing.does: Research benchmark of 23 tasks across five attack surfaces, testing nine mechanisms across six harnesses including Claude Code
existing.lacks: A tool a user runs against their own local hook configuration

score_reasons.buildability: Hooks are commands that read a JSON tool-call on stdin and answer with exit code or decision, so reading settings, piping synthetic payloads and tabulating results is a small, well-bounded CLI.
score_reasons.insight: Treating hooks as a security control that needs a firewall-style self-test is a sensible connection the evidence supports, but it is not surprising.
score_reasons.differentiation: Plugin authors test their own hooks and a benchmark exists for research, but nothing tests a user's stacked config locally; plugin authors could add this.
score_reasons.grounding: The person, the moment, the blocked categories and the benchmark trace to evidence; the probe count and the dry-invocation mechanism do not.

buildability_reasons: Claude Code hooks are configured in local settings files and invoked with JSON on stdin, so they can be called directly without the agent.
Probes are only payloads handed to hooks; nothing destructive is ever executed.
Output is a pass/fail table, which needs no UI or external service.
Matcher semantics and multiple settings scopes (user, project, plugin) add some edge cases.
risks: Hook pipelines may be hard to invoke dry: some hooks have side effects, need env vars, or depend on the plugin's runtime.
Plugin authors or Claude Code itself may add a built-in hook test.
The probes may be too generic and miss obfuscated variants, which would give users false confidence.
Hook config formats and plugin hook locations may change between Claude Code versions.
brief: Developers who have stacked guard hooks from a couple of Claude Code plugins have no way to know whether force-pushes, destructive commands and secret writes are actually blocked before they let the agent run unattended, and they don't want to find out on a real repo. Build something they can run from the terminal that reads their own hook configuration, hands each hook a set of benchmark-style destructive tool calls without ever executing them, and prints a pass/fail table of which probes were blocked and which got through.
grounding: A developer who installed guard hooks from two Claude Code plugins asks how to verify that force-pushes and secret writes are actually blocked before letting the agent run unattended; they do not want to find out on a real repo.
skillkeel-starter v0.1.12 is an MIT Claude Code plugin with three guard hooks that block destructive commands, force-pushes and secret writes; the author says it is a guard, not a sandbox.
HarnessSecurity-Bench introduces a benchmark of 23 tasks across five attack surfaces and tests nine mechanisms across six harnesses, including Claude Code.
Smallest useful v1: a script that runs twenty probes through the local hook pipeline and prints a pass/fail table.
Thesis: hooks are a security control and deserve a self-test; the benchmark supplies the probes.
Cheapest test: run it against five users' hook configs; it is real if it finds at least one unblocked destructive probe in two of them.
cheapest_test: Run it against five users' Claude Code hook configs; it is real if it finds at least one unblocked destructive probe in two of them.

claims.claim: fires destructive commands at your hook config
claims.interpreted: Sends synthetic tool-call payloads describing destructive commands to the hook commands only; the destructive commands themselves are never executed.
claims.why: The hook's decision is the thing under test, so it can be measured without running anything dangerous.

claims.interpreted: Reports which of its own probes the configured hooks did not block. That is a lower bound on exposure, not proof that everything else is blocked.
claims.why: Finding even one unblocked force-push or secret write is the outcome the developer is asking for.

claims.interpreted: A built-in probe set covering destructive commands, force-pushes and secret writes, modelled on the benchmark's attack surfaces but not a reproduction of it, with room for user-added probes.

setting.means: Path to an optional file of additional user-defined probes

claims.why: The value is a known-bad input set to test against, not fidelity to a specific paper or count.

claims.claim: runs through the local hook pipeline
claims.interpreted: Invokes each matching configured hook command with a per-hook time limit; a hook that times out or errors is reported as such, not as a pass.

setting.means: How long to wait for each hook before marking the probe as errored

claims.why: A hung or crashing hook is itself something the developer needs to see before going unattended.
